questions.prompt: Two inspectors label 400 crops for a rare defect. They give the same label to 372 crops, and Cohen's kappa is 0.28. What does the pair of numbers tell you?
options: The labels are reliable, because 93% agreement is high
The inspectors mostly agree by both saying "no"; on the defect itself they barely agree
Kappa was computed wrongly, because it cannot be far below raw agreement
One inspector is careless and should be replaced
questions.explanation: With a rare class most agreement comes from both saying "no"; kappa removes that chance agreement and shows what is left.
misconceptions: Reads raw agreement without asking how much of it chance alone would produce
Expects kappa to track raw agreement, which fails exactly when one label dominates
Blames a person for a disagreement that the definition produced

questions.prompt: A guideline says: "Label rutting when the wheel path looks sunken." Agreement between annotators is poor. Which rewrite is most likely to raise it?
options: "Label rutting when the wheel path looks clearly sunken to a trained eye."
"Label rutting only when you are certain."
"Label rutting when a 2-metre straightedge across the lane would show a gap of 10 mm or more; if the depth cannot be judged from the frame, flag it."
"Label rutting as in the three example pictures."
questions.explanation: A definition that can be measured or counted, with a rule for the undecidable case, is one that two strangers can apply alike.
misconceptions: Adds emphasis, not a criterion: "clearly" is still a judgement of resemblance
Turns uncertainty into silent negatives, which hides the borderline cases from the data
Relies on examples alone, which cannot settle a case that sits between them

questions.prompt: A dataset holds 9,000 frames from 300 road segments; each segment was filmed on several passes. You need a test set that predicts performance on roads never surveyed. How do you draw it?
options: Draw 15% of the frames at random
Draw 15% of the frames at random, then delete exact duplicate files
Draw 15% of the passes at random
Draw 15% of the segments and take all their frames
questions.explanation: The model must generalise over roads, so the road segment is the unit that stays whole; frames and passes of one segment share surface, markings and defects.
misconceptions: Treats frames as independent although frames of one spot are near-copies
Believes leakage is only byte-identical files; near-duplicates and same-site frames remain
Keeps passes together but still places the same segment on both sides

questions.prompt: After re-splitting by road segment, 120 frames have no segment id and no near-duplicate that has one. What do you do with them?
options: Put them in the training set, where a few extra frames can only help
Leave them out of training, validation and test
Put them in the test set, to make it larger
Assign each to a random segment so that no frame is wasted
questions.explanation: A frame of unknown origin may share its road with the other side of the split wherever it is placed, so it is safe on neither side.
misconceptions: Assumes leakage only matters in the test set: a training frame from a test segment leaks just the same
Trades the honesty of the test for its size
Invents the group key, which makes the split report false

questions.prompt: A class "arrow marking: turn left" is added to a road-marking classifier. Which augmentation must be removed from the pipeline for this class?
options: Random brightness changes
A small random scale change
A left-right mirror
Gaussian blur
questions.explanation: A mirrored left-turn arrow is a right-turn arrow: the transform changes the property the label is defined by.
misconceptions: Assumes photometric changes threaten a label that is defined by shape and direction
Confuses a change of size with a change of meaning
Treats a softer picture as a different class, though the arrow still points left

questions.prompt: True or false: if a perceptual hash finds no near-duplicate pairs across the training and test sets, the split is free of leakage.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A hash finds frames that look almost identical; frames of the same site under another light, or of a neighbouring spot, share information without matching.
misconceptions: Equates leakage with near-identical pixels, although shared sites leak without them

questions.prompt: On 40 night crops, backbone A scores 80% with a 95% interval of 68% to 92%, and backbone B scores 85% with 73% to 95%. What may you conclude about night?
options: B is better at night by five points
A and B are equally good at night
This test cannot separate the two at night; more night crops or a paired comparison is needed
The intervals are too wide, so the bootstrap was done incorrectly
questions.explanation: Overlapping intervals on a small slice mean the evidence does not distinguish the models; that is a statement about the test, not about the models.
misconceptions: Reads a point estimate as a finding on forty crops
Mistakes "not shown to differ" for "shown to be equal"
Expects narrow intervals regardless of sample size

questions.prompt: With 300 labelled crops, a linear probe on a frozen backbone reaches 84% and full fine-tuning reaches 82%. With 3,000 labels full fine-tuning reaches 93%. Labelling 3,000 crops takes two weeks. The pilot needs a model on Monday. What do you ship first?
options: The fully fine-tuned model on 300 labels, because full fine-tuning is the stronger method
The linear probe on 300 labels, and start labelling towards 3,000
Nothing until 3,000 labels exist
A model trained from scratch on the 300 labels, to avoid depending on pretrained weights
questions.explanation: At this label budget the probe is at least as good and far cheaper; the table also shows that labels, not more training, buy the next gain.
misconceptions: Ranks methods in general instead of reading the numbers at this label budget
Lets the better future result block a usable present one
Discards pretraining when labels are scarcest, which is when it helps most

questions.prompt: A zero-shot image-text model scores 71% on five defect classes with well-written prompts. Your fine-tuned classifier, built on 2,000 labelled crops, scores 74%. How do you report this?
options: As a success: the fine-tuned model has the higher score
As a failure of the zero-shot model, which did not reach 74%
As 74%, without mentioning the zero-shot result, since it used no training
As a three-point gain over a floor that cost no labels, which questions the value of the labelling so far
questions.explanation: The floor is what the department gets for free; the worth of 2,000 labels is the distance above it, and three points is little.
misconceptions: Compares against nothing, so any trained model looks like progress
Judges the baseline by the wrong standard: a floor is there to be beaten, and it nearly was not
Omits the comparison that tells the reader what the labels bought

questions.prompt: You compare a convolutional backbone and a vision transformer on defect crops. Which setup makes the comparison fair?
options: The same training crops, test crops, input size and number of passes, each with a learning rate tuned for it on validation data
The same learning rate for both, whatever it does to each
Each on the input size from its own paper, tested on its own split
The transformer on more passes, because transformers need more data
questions.explanation: Hold the data, the budget and the test fixed; tune what is specific to each model on validation data, never on the test set.
misconceptions: Confuses identical hyperparameters with a fair comparison: one learning rate can cripple one model
Changes the test along with the model, so the scores are not comparable
Gives one model a larger budget and then compares the results

questions.prompt: A backbone's code is under Apache-2.0 and its pretrained weights are under CC-BY-NC-4.0. A contractor will run it on roadside units for a city under a paid contract. May these weights be deployed?
options: Yes: the code licence is permissive and covers the whole model
Yes: a city is a public body, so its use is non-commercial
Not under these terms: the weights carry a non-commercial licence and this is paid operation
Yes, after fine-tuning: fine-tuned weights are a new work free of the original terms
questions.explanation: What runs on the unit is the weights, and their licence governs; a paid contract is commercial use, so other weights or another licence are needed.
misconceptions: Assumes the code licence extends to the weights, which are licensed separately
Decides commercial use by who the client is, not by the nature of the operation
Assumes fine-tuning removes the terms of the weights it started from

questions.prompt: A pothole detector has an average precision of 0.91 at IoU 0.5 and 0.48 at IoU 0.75. What does the gap point to?
options: Many potholes are missed entirely
Boxes sit on the potholes but do not fit them tightly, or the labelled boxes are inconsistent in tightness
The detector confuses potholes with patches
The score threshold is set too high
questions.explanation: A box that is roughly right passes at 0.5 and fails at 0.75; that is a localisation problem in the model or in the labels.
misconceptions: A missed object lowers the score at both thresholds alike
A class confusion is an error at every overlap threshold
Average precision sweeps over all score thresholds, so no single threshold explains it

questions.prompt: After a software update the detector reports three overlapping boxes on most potholes, and average precision at IoU 0.5 falls sharply although nothing was retrained. What is the first thing to check?
options: The non-maximum suppression threshold, which may have been loosened or switched off
The learning rate of the last training run
Whether the test labels were changed
The class weights of the loss
questions.explanation: Several boxes per object after an unchanged model is the signature of missing or loose suppression; each extra box counts as a false positive.
misconceptions: Looks into training although the model did not change
Suspects the labels, which would not multiply the boxes per object
Looks into training although the model did not change

questions.prompt: A detection is labelled "patch" and overlaps a ground-truth pothole with IoU 0.82. No other detection touches that pothole. Which error type is it?
options: Localisation
Duplicate
Missed
Class
questions.explanation: The box fits; only the class is wrong. A fix lies in more examples of the confused pair or a clearer class definition.
misconceptions: The overlap of 0.82 is well above the threshold, so the box is not the problem
A duplicate needs a better-scoring detection already on the same object
The pothole was found, with the wrong name

questions.prompt: An oracle analysis of a detector gives these gains in average precision if each error type were fully fixed: duplicates +0.06, class +0.01, localisation +0.03, missed +0.05. Tightening suppression takes ten minutes; collecting data for missed defects takes three weeks. What do you do first?
options: Collect data for the missed defects, because recall matters most
Tighten suppression, measure again, then plan the data collection from the new table
Relabel all boxes for localisation
Work on class confusion, since it is the hardest
questions.explanation: The largest gain is also the cheapest; and fixing one type moves the others, so the table is measured again before three weeks are spent.
misconceptions: Chooses by a general belief rather than by the gains and costs on the table
Picks a costly fix with half the gain of a free one
Chooses the smallest gain on the table

questions.prompt: A crack segmenter scores IoU 0.55. Its masks follow every crack, shifted by about one pixel. The cracks are two to three pixels wide. How should the result be reported?
options: As poor: an IoU of 0.55 means nearly half of the cracks are missed
As IoU 0.55 together with a score that allows a small tolerance, and example masks
As pixel accuracy, which is above 97%
As Dice only, because it is the higher number
questions.explanation: On thin structures a one-pixel shift costs a large share of the overlap; a tolerance score and pictures show what the plain IoU hides.
misconceptions: Reads IoU as the fraction of objects found, which it is not
Uses a score that an empty mask would also reach when cracks are a few percent of pixels
Chooses the metric by how flattering it is

questions.prompt: True or false: a thresholding baseline that marks dark pixels as cracks is not worth scoring once a neural segmenter is available.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The baseline costs minutes, gives the number to beat, and its failures by lighting show what the learned model must add.
misconceptions: Assumes a learned model is better by default, without a number to show by how much or where

questions.prompt: On a clip with 20 vehicles crossing the line, a tracker reports a count of 20 and 15 identity switches. The traffic team will use it only for counts on this camera. What do you tell them?
options: The count cannot be trusted, because the identities are wrong
The tracker is ready for any use
For counting on this camera the evidence supports it; it is not fit for uses that follow a vehicle, such as travel time
Identity switches do not matter for any application
questions.explanation: A switch costs a count only when it happens at the line; uses that need one identity per vehicle are a different requirement.
misconceptions: Assumes every identity switch corrupts the count
Generalises from one metric to all uses
Dismisses a metric that other applications depend on

questions.prompt: In slow traffic a counter reports 31 vehicles where 22 crossed. Its rule adds one whenever a box centre moves from above the line to below it. What is the most likely cause, and the fix?
options: Missed detections; lower the detector's score threshold
Boxes jitter back and forth across the line; count each track at most once
The line is too close to the camera; move it further away
False detections; raise the score threshold
questions.explanation: A slow vehicle's centre crosses the line several times as its box jitters; counting once per track removes the repeats.
misconceptions: Missed detections lose counts; they do not add nine
Moves the line without removing the cause, which is the rule
False alarms rarely travel across a line; the pattern is tied to slow traffic

questions.prompt: At night the detector misses a vehicle in about one frame in eight. The tracker closes a track as soon as one frame has no matching detection. What happens to the count, and which setting addresses it?
options: Counts rise; require more hits before a track is reported
Counts are unaffected; nothing needs to change
Tracks break at misses, and a break at the line loses a count; let a track survive a few frames without a detection
Counts fall; lower the overlap threshold for matching to zero
questions.explanation: A track that ends just before the line and restarts just after it never crosses; a little patience bridges single missed frames.
misconceptions: Mixes up the remedy for short-lived false tracks with the remedy for broken true ones
Overlooks that a break exactly at the line removes a crossing
Matches anything to anything, which trades broken tracks for swapped ones

questions.prompt: Which pair of numbers is the evidence that a counting service works on a set of clips with ground truth?
options: Detector average precision and frames per second
Count error per clip and the number of identity switches
The total count over all clips and the average track length
Training loss and validation loss of the detector
questions.explanation: Count error per clip shows whether the product is right, clip by clip; identity switches show how fragile the tracks behind it are.
misconceptions: Measures a component, not the count the service delivers
A total hides overcounts in one clip cancelling undercounts in another
Describes training, not the behaviour of the service

questions.prompt: A roadside unit must process each frame within 60 ms. Measured on the unit: median 41 ms, 95th percentile 74 ms. Does the model meet the budget?
options: Yes: the median is well inside the budget
Yes: the average of the two numbers is under 60 ms
No: one frame in twenty takes longer than the budget allows
It cannot be said without the maximum
questions.explanation: A per-frame budget is about the slow frames; at the 95th percentile the model is over, so frames are late or dropped.
misconceptions: Judges a tail requirement by the typical case
Averages two percentiles, which describes no frame at all
Waits for a noisier statistic when the percentile already answers

questions.prompt: You quantise a detector to 8-bit integers. The file shrinks to a quarter and latency falls by 40%. What must happen before it replaces the 32-bit model?
options: Nothing: quantisation does not change predictions
Its accuracy is measured again on the same validation frames, by condition
It is retrained from scratch
Its input resolution is raised to make up for the lost precision
questions.explanation: Every weight and activation changed a little; only a measurement on the same frames tells whether small or low-contrast objects were lost.
misconceptions: Assumes rounding to 256 levels is harmless for every model
Prescribes a costly remedy before knowing whether there is a loss
Spends the latency gain on a guess

questions.prompt: An exported model gives outputs within 0.00001 of the original in your test. On the device, the same file detects almost nothing. Where do you look first?
options: In the exported graph, for an operation that was converted wrongly
In the training data, for label noise
In the device's preprocessing: channel order, value range and resizing
In the model's architecture, which may be too large for the device
questions.explanation: The file is proven by the parity test; what differs on the device is what is fed to it, and preprocessing mismatches fail silently.
misconceptions: Re-examines the part the parity test has just cleared
Looks at training although the original model works
A model that is too large runs slowly or not at all; it does not run and see nothing

questions.prompt: Benchmark rows that meet the size limit: 192 pixels, 71 ms, AP 0.88; 160 pixels, 52 ms, AP 0.84; 128 pixels, 36 ms, AP 0.66. The budget is 60 ms at the 95th percentile, which these latencies are. Which operating point do you choose?
options: 192 pixels: accuracy comes first
128 pixels: the fastest is the safest
160 pixels: the most accurate row inside the budget
None: the budget should be renegotiated to 71 ms
questions.explanation: The budget is a constraint and accuracy the objective: take the best accuracy among the rows that fit.
misconceptions: Treats the budget as a preference: a model that misses it does not run on the unit
Gives up 18 points of accuracy for speed nobody asked for
Reopens the requirement although a row meets it

questions.prompt: To measure the effect of rain on a detector you can (a) compare a clean test set with a different set of rainy frames, or (b) apply rain to the same test frames. Why does (b) give a tighter estimate of the drop?
options: It uses more frames
Each frame is its own control, so differences between scenes cancel
Synthetic rain is easier for a detector than real rain
It avoids the need for ground truth
questions.explanation: With paired frames the only thing that differs is the condition; with two sets, the difficulty of the scenes differs as well.
misconceptions: The number of frames can be the same in both designs
Makes a claim about difficulty that the design does not rest on, and that may be false
Both designs need ground truth to compute a score

questions.prompt: The release rule says: a condition passes when the upper end of the 95% interval of its accuracy drop is at most 0.10. For glare the drop is 0.06 with an interval of 0.01 to 0.14, on 60 frames. What is the decision?
options: Pass: the drop of 0.06 is below 0.10
Fail for now: the upper end is 0.14; test more glare frames or apply the fallback for failed conditions
Pass: most of the interval lies below 0.10
Fail permanently: the detector cannot handle glare
questions.explanation: The rule is written on the upper end so that a small test cannot pass by luck; more frames narrow the interval and may change the outcome.
misconceptions: Applies the rule to the estimate instead of the bound it names
Replaces the stated rule by an impression of the interval
Reads an inconclusive test as a proven failure

questions.prompt: A pole camera was knocked and now looks at the road from a different angle. Its brightness and sharpness are unchanged, and its counts fall slowly. Which monitor would have caught it on the first days?
options: Mean brightness against the first week
Sharpness against the first week
The position of fixed scene features, such as lane markings, against their position at installation
The model's average confidence
questions.explanation: A moved camera changes where fixed things appear, not how bright or sharp the picture is; a monitor on their position sees it at once.
misconceptions: Watches a statistic the fault does not move
Watches a statistic the fault does not move
Average confidence drifts for many reasons and may not move at all when objects are merely smaller

questions.prompt: Faces and plates are blurred before frames are stored. At the detector's default threshold 84% of them are blurred and 1% of the image area is affected; at a low threshold 99% are blurred and 3% of the area. Which setting fits a rule that nothing readable is stored?
options: The default threshold: fewer false alarms means a cleaner archive
The default threshold: 84% is a high recall
No blurring: the frames are only used internally
The low threshold: a blurred patch of wall costs little, a stored readable plate breaks the rule
questions.explanation: The two errors have unequal costs, so the operating point is chosen for recall, and the remaining 1% is stated in the model card.
misconceptions: Optimises the error that costs nothing here
Accepts one readable face or plate in six
Mistakes internal use for an exemption: stored personal data is stored personal data

questions.prompt: Which statement belongs in the results section of a model card for a roadside pothole detector?
options: "The model achieves state-of-the-art accuracy."
"AP at IoU 0.5 is 0.89 on clean frames; under heavy rain it falls by 0.12 (0.07 to 0.18); night detections go to an inspector before a crew is sent."
"The model was trained for 30 passes with AdamW."
"The model should be used responsibly."
questions.explanation: A result names the metric, the condition, the size of the effect with its interval, and what happens under that condition.
misconceptions: Makes a claim with no metric, data or condition behind it
Describes training, which belongs in another section
States an intention that no reader can check or act on

questions.prompt: True or false: if a detector meets its accuracy target on the whole test set, it meets it in every district of the city.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: An average can hide a district with older roads or more dust where the model is much worse; reporting by district is how that is noticed.
misconceptions: Assumes an overall average holds for every subgroup
